title: Confirm the surface before work: natural stone, terrazzo or engineered stone
audience: Stone and terrazzo restoration technicians, leading hands and supervisors who assess a surface before any abrasive, chemical or sealing step
learningOutcomes: Identify whether a surface is natural stone, terrazzo or possibly engineered stone using documents and non-destructive observation
Explain why a surface that cannot be confirmed is a stop-work case
Record the identification basis, photograph the surface and state a proceed or stop decision
Refuse any test that cuts, grinds or scratches the surface to identify it
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: DEWR, Prohibition on the use of engineered stone (no date shown); ASEA, Engineered stone prohibition (no date shown); SA Government, Engineered stone ban (title dated 1 July 2024; no publication date shown); WorkSafe Victoria, Working with engineered stone (reviewed 27 August 2024); Safe Work Australia, When does a PCBU need to notify the WHS regulator of plans to process legacy engineered stone (August 2025); Safe Work Australia, Working with silica and silica containing products (national guidance) (February 2022).

instruction.heading: Why identification comes first
instruction.body: The surface type decides what you are allowed to do. Natural stone such as marble, granite, limestone and slate, and terrazzo, can be honed, polished and sealed under the controls taught in this course. Engineered stone benchtops, panels and slabs are different. The national prohibition on their use, supply and manufacture started on 1 July 2024. Installed engineered stone does not have to be removed, but processing it is restricted, and some legacy processing needs notice to the WHS regulator before the work starts (see “The engineered stone prohibition and what it means on a job”). Because the outcome is so different, the first task on every job is to confirm the material, not to assume it. A kitchen benchtop that looks like granite may be engineered stone. A client who says it is granite is giving an opinion, which is useful information but is not an identification.

instruction.heading: Checks that do not damage the surface
instruction.body: Start with paper. Look for the product label, the installer's documents, the warranty card, the supplier invoice, the builder's specification and any maintenance guide the client has kept. Then look at the surface from a normal viewing distance and in good light. Engineered stone often shows a very even colour and speckle pattern repeated across a large area, and a sheen that looks uniform from every angle. Natural granite shows a crystal structure with variation in grain, and natural marble shows veining that changes across the slab. Terrazzo shows chips set in a matrix. These cues are only reasons to stop and check. They are not a reliable test on their own, and a surface that looks like granite can still be engineered stone. Do not scratch, grind, cut, wet-rub with abrasives or take a sample to test the surface. Cutting, grinding and sanding are named as silica dust-generating processes in the national guidance. Those actions can also change the surface. If the material is still uncertain after the document and visual checks, treat it as engineered stone and stop.

instruction.heading: What to record and who decides
instruction.body: Record the basis for your decision. A documented identification means a product label, an installer or manufacturer document, or a written confirmation from the responsible person who has the authority to give it. Photograph the surface, any label or document, and any marks or cracks. Write the decision, the date and your name. Terrazzo needs one more point. This is a precaution, not a regulator's statement. Refer any doubt about terrazzo to the responsible person and the state regulator before work.

procedure: Read the work order and write down what the client has said about the material.
Check the documents: product label, installer or manufacturer documents, warranty card, specification and invoice.
Observe the surface from a normal distance and in good light without touching it or disturbing it.
Compare the observations with the cues in this lesson, and note which cues you saw and which you did not.
Record the identification basis, take photographs of the surface, labels and any marks, and write the decision with the date and your name.
If the material is confirmed as natural stone or terrazzo, record the decision to proceed and continue to the surface assessment in “Pre-work surface assessment and test patches”.
If the material is unknown or might be engineered stone, do not touch the surface further.

workedExamples.situation: A twelve-year-old kitchen benchtop in a unit. The client says it is granite and the work order asks for honing and sealing. There is no installer document, no label is visible under the sink, and the surface has a very uniform, fine and even speckle with no visible variation in grain across the whole top.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the technician do before any abrasive step, and what should be recorded?
workedExamples.reasoning: The correct decision is to stop, photograph the surface and any location where a label might be, record the basis as unknown, and notify the supervisor so that a documented identification can be sought.

equipmentAndPpe: Good torch or daylight for viewing the surface without disturbing it
Camera or phone for dated photographs of the surface, labels and marks
Job record sheet or electronic form for the identification basis and decision
Standard site PPE for the work area, as set by the site induction (no abrasive or cutting equipment is used for identification)

commonErrors.error: Accepting the client's word as the identification and starting to hone or polish.
commonErrors.prevention: Require a document or a written confirmation from the responsible person before any abrasive or chemical step.

commonErrors.error: Scratching a corner or using a file or grinder to see what the surface is made of.
commonErrors.prevention: Never test by scratching, grinding, cutting or sampling. Those tests create silica dust and can change the surface.

commonErrors.error: Treating terrazzo as safe because it looks like stone.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat terrazzo as silica-containing until its composition is known, and apply the silica controls in “Respirable crystalline silica: where it comes from and why it matters” and “Dust controls: wet methods, extraction, isolation and housekeeping”.

commonErrors.error: Using appearance cues as proof that the surface is natural stone.
commonErrors.prevention: Use cues only to decide whether to stop and check. A cue cannot replace a documented identification.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Engineered stone benchtops, panels and slabs are subject to a national prohibition that started on 1 July 2024. Installed engineered stone does not have to be removed. Work that removes, repairs, modifies or disposes of installed engineered stone is restricted, and some legacy processing requires notification to the WHS regulator before the work starts. This lesson does not give permission for any engineered stone work and does not grant a licence, permit or exemption.
Stop-work rule: if the surface is not identified as natural stone or terrazzo on a documented basis, do not abrade, cut, chemically treat or seal it.
Check the WHS regulator for your state before any engineered stone work and before taking on any job that may involve it.

qualityStandard: The material is identified before any abrasive, chemical or sealing step, and the identification basis is recorded.
No identification test damages, cuts, grinds or scratches the surface.
Terrazzo is recorded as silica-containing until its composition is known.
Every stop decision has a named escalation and a dated record.
documentationEvidence: Identification basis: document reference, written confirmation or visual observation recorded as unidentified.
Dated photographs of the surface, labels, and any marks or cracks
Decision to proceed or stop, with name and date
Escalation record when the decision is to stop
summary: Confirm the material before any abrasive, chemical or sealing step.
Documents and written confirmation count as identification; appearance alone does not.
Never test by scratching, grinding, cutting or sampling.
Terrazzo is silica-containing until its composition is known.
When in doubt, stop, record and escalate.

knowledgeChecks.question: A client says a kitchen benchtop is granite. There is no document and the surface looks very uniform. What is the correct action?
options: Stop, record the basis and photographs, and refer to the responsible person before any abrasive step
Proceed with honing because the client has confirmed the material type in writing on the day of the job
Make a small scratch with a file to check the surface and the colour underneath it very quickly today
Apply sealer to see whether the surface absorbs it and how much it takes up quickly on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about terrazzo is correct for this course?
options: Terrazzo is treated as silica-containing until its composition is known
Terrazzo is always natural stone and needs no silica controls
Terrazzo is always engineered stone and cannot be worked on

knowledgeChecks.question: Which action is an acceptable way to identify a surface?
options: Scratching a corner with a steel scribe to see the colour, the grain and the sheen of the stone surface
Grinding a small patch to see the colour, the grain, the sheen and the finish of the stone surface
Reviewing the product label, installer documents or a written confirmation from the responsible person
Cutting a sample to examine its structure and the stone's inside under a bright lamp on the site today

knowledgeChecks.question: When may a job move past identification to surface assessment?
options: When the client says they are confident about the material
When the technician believes the surface looks like marble
When natural stone or terrazzo is confirmed and the basis is recorded

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should appearance cues alone not decide the material?
options: Appearance cues are reasons to stop and check, not a verified identification
Appearance cues are a legally reliable test for the material type and finish
Appearance cues show which state licence applies to the job on the day
Appearance cues show the silica level of the surface in the air nearby today
